# Installing

The console is a **standalone binary**. Using it does not require a Rust
toolchain.

## Download a release binary

Releases are published on the version schedule by release-please, and each
release carries a linux `x86_64` binary plus its SHA-256 sum:

```bash
gh release download --repo thewoolleyman/livespec-console-beads-fabro \
  --pattern 'livespec-console-beads-fabro-*-x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu'
```

Verify the checksum, then put the binary on your `PATH`:

```bash
gh release download --repo thewoolleyman/livespec-console-beads-fabro \
  --pattern 'livespec-console-beads-fabro-*-x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu.sha256'
sha256sum -c livespec-console-beads-fabro-*-x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu.sha256

chmod +x livespec-console-beads-fabro-*-x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu
mv livespec-console-beads-fabro-*-x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu \
  ~/.local/bin/livespec-console-beads-fabro
```

Or fetch the binary for your platform from the repository's Releases page.
Only linux `x86_64` is published today.

> **Acceptance-verified on linux `x86_64` only, for the download path.** The
> published `v0.2.0` asset was downloaded with the commands above, checksum-
> verified, and run from an arbitrary working directory outside any git
> repository, against two different repositories — each launched from inside
> its own checkout, which `v0.2.0` required. That is the extent of what has
> been exercised: one host, one architecture, the `serve` read path.
> Other platforms have no published asset and no acceptance run — use the
> source build below.
>
> **The acceptance run has not been repeated since.** The globs above fetch
> the CURRENT release, `v0.4.0`, which is a superset of the acceptance-run
> build — it carries the cross-repo fix described under
> [Running against a different repository](#running-against-a-different-repository),
> so it does not need the `cd` that `v0.2.0` did. That fix is
> covered by the test suite, not by a download-and-run acceptance exercise;
> no published asset after `v0.2.0` has been through one.

## Build from source

Building is also the path for contributors and for platforms with no
published asset:

```bash
cargo build --release --package livespec-console-beads-fabro
# → target/release/livespec-console-beads-fabro
```

From a source checkout the console is normally launched through `just`, which
wraps it in the family credential wrapper:

```bash
just tui
```

`just serve` is an alias for the same recipe, and extra arguments pass
through. See [Overview and quick start](overview-quickstart.md).

## Prerequisites

The console observes live state by shelling out to the orchestrator and
reading its journals, so a useful session needs:

- **A reachable Beads tenant** — the server-side Dolt tenant must exist, with
  the credential wrapper on `PATH` so `BEADS_DOLT_PASSWORD` is injected. Run
  the console under the wrapper:

  ```bash
  /usr/local/bin/with-livespec-env.sh -- livespec-console-beads-fabro serve
  ```

# Installing

The console is a **standalone binary**. Using it does not require a Rust
toolchain.

## Download a release binary

Releases are published on the version schedule by release-please, and each
release carries a linux `x86_64` binary plus its SHA-256 sum:

```bash
gh release download --repo thewoolleyman/livespec-console-beads-fabro \
  --pattern 'livespec-console-beads-fabro-*-x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu'
```

Verify the checksum, then put the binary on your `PATH`:

```bash
gh release download --repo thewoolleyman/livespec-console-beads-fabro \
  --pattern 'livespec-console-beads-fabro-*-x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu.sha256'
sha256sum -c livespec-console-beads-fabro-*-x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu.sha256

chmod +x livespec-console-beads-fabro-*-x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu
mv livespec-console-beads-fabro-*-x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu \
  ~/.local/bin/livespec-console-beads-fabro
```

Or fetch the binary for your platform from the repository's Releases page.
Only linux `x86_64` is published today.

> published `v0.2.0` asset was downloaded with the commands above, checksum-
> verified, and run from an arbitrary working directory outside any git
> repository, against two different repositories — each launched from inside

> source build below.

published asset:

# Overview and quick start

## What the console is

The console is the human operator's view of a LiveSpec factory. Work flows
through the orchestrator autonomously up to the points where a human must
decide something; the console is where you see that state and make those
decisions.

It owns the operator view across:

- LiveSpec spec-side lifecycle state
- Beads work-items and their seven lifecycle lanes
- Dispatcher waves and journals
- Fabro runs and human gates
- GitHub pull requests and checks
- work held for explicit approval rather than autonomous dispatch

Internally it is a single Rust executable with an event-sourced core, pull
adapters with durable checkpoint/backfill, and SQLite WAL as the durable event
log. The TUI is the first frontend; a GUI could reuse the same command/event
backend later.

**The console commands and observes; it never writes.** It holds no setting
state of its own, derives every value it shows from a published read surface,
and issues every write through the orchestrator's `drive` API — never by
editing the orchestrator's `.livespec.jsonc` or the ledger directly.

## Quick start

Launch the interactive TUI from a source checkout:

```bash
just tui
```

or, from an installed binary, under the credential wrapper:

```bash
/usr/local/bin/with-livespec-env.sh -- livespec-console-beads-fabro serve
```

The console starts the full-screen TUI when standard output is a terminal.
If stdout is not a terminal, or you pass `--preview`, it prints a one-shot
text report instead of taking over the screen.

### Find what needs you

Focus starts on the **Views** menu on the left. `↑`/`↓` walk it; `Enter` or
`→` moves focus into the content pane.

The **Attention** view is the point of the console: it lists exactly the items
waiting on a human — pending approval, acceptance review, and blocked-on-human.
If it is empty, the factory does not need you.

### Act on an item

With an item selected in **Attention**, the per-item valves are bound to
single keys:

| Key | Action |
|---|---|
| `p` | approve |
| `c` | accept |
| `r` | reject (warned as dangerous) |

Each opens a confirmation modal; `Enter` confirms, `Esc` cancels. Every one is
issued through the orchestrator's `drive` API.

### Work the board

The **Lanes** view shows all seven lanes. In the content pane `Enter` drills
into a lane, and `↑`/`↓` then select an individual work-item. Inside a
drilled-in lane you also get `s` — **move to status** — which offers the
statuses that item may legally be driven to.

### Drain the ready queue

Press `:` to open the command palette, type `drain` (or `drain ready queue`),
then `Enter`.

content.text:
Two separate things are on that screen, and up/down only drives one of them — that's the confusion.

## The `Menu:` bar at the very top is *not* what up/down controls

`Work item · Factory · View · Help · File` is a permanent, always-rendered bar. It's inert until you **open** it:

- Press **`v`** (or **Left arrow** while focus is on the Views pane) to open it.
- Once open: **Left/Right** move between the top nodes (Work item ↔ Factory ↔ …), **Up/Down** move within the dropdown, **Enter** selects, **Esc** closes.

## The `Views [focus]` pane *is* what up/down drives

Focus starts here (that's the `[focus]` tag). The list is vertical, top-to-bottom:

**Attention → Spec → Lanes → Events → Repos → Settings**

Up/down walk that list. Your selection is sitting on **Attention**, which is the **top item** — so **up has nowhere to go and does nothing** (there's no wrap-around). That's exactly why it "seems intuitive but doesn't work."

**Try `↓` (down)** — it'll move you Attention → Spec → Lanes, and you'll see the selection move. Then:

- **Enter** or **→** dives focus into the content pane (the middle **Attention** list) so you can select individual items.
- **Esc** or **←** takes focus back to Views (← from Views opens the menu bar, per above).

So: down works, up is just capped at the top of the Views list, and the top `Menu:` bar needs `v` to wake up. If up-at-the-top being silently inert feels wrong to you, that's a reasonable dogfooding finding — I can file it (e.g. wrap-around, or a cue that you're at the top).

# Dispatch action investigation — why it shows "not available" for a Needs Attention item

## Summary of root cause

There are **two** dispatch ActionSpecs in the registry. The per-item one — `dispatch-selected-item` — is deliberately gated to the **drilled-in Lanes surface only**. When you select a work-item in the **Needs Attention** view, the console builds its availability context with `surface = ActionSurface::Attention`, and the closure `matches!(ctx.surface, ActionSurface::LaneDrill)` is `false`, so the action is unavailable there **by design** — regardless of the item's lane or admission policy. Dispatch-from-Attention (via this registry action) is not intended to exist; per-item dispatch is a Lanes-view-drilled-in verb.

---

## 1. The ActionSpec for dispatch

There are two, both at `/data/projects/livespec-console-beads-fabro/crates/console-application/src/action_registry.rs`.

**`dispatch-ready`** — the selection-less factory drain (lines 470–480):
```rust
ActionSpec {
    id: "dispatch-ready",
    label: "Dispatch ready work",
    hint_token: "",
    hotkeys: &[],
    menu_path: &["Factory", "Dispatch"],
    parameter: None,
    availability_summary: "Available when the board has at least one ready work-item.",
    availability: |ctx| ctx.ready_work_item_count > 0,
    staging: ActionStaging::FactoryDrain,
},
```

**`dispatch-selected-item`** — the per-item dispatch (lines 481–493), which is the one relevant to your question:
```rust
ActionSpec {
    id: "dispatch-selected-item",
    label: "Dispatch selected item",
    hint_token: "",
    hotkeys: &[],
    menu_path: &["Factory", "Dispatch"],
    parameter: None,
    availability_summary: "Available for a selected ready work-item in a drilled-in lane.",
    availability: |ctx| {
        ctx.lane == Lane::Ready && matches!(ctx.surface, ActionSurface::LaneDrill)
    },
    staging: ActionStaging::FactoryDispatchItem,
},
```

**What the closure checks:** two conjuncts, both must hold —
1. `ctx.lane == Lane::Ready` — the selected item's lifecycle lane must be `ready`.
2. `ctx.surface == ActionSurface::LaneDrill` — the selection must live on the **drilled-in Lanes** surface, not the Attention inbox.

Neither hotkey nor hint token is set (it is menu/invoker-only, reachable through `Factory > Dispatch`). It has no admission-policy or pending-approval component; it is purely lane + surface.

The test at lines 1364–1388 (`dispatch_selected_item_is_gated_on_a_selected_ready_item`) pins this: a Ready `LaneDrill` context yields `true`; a Backlog one yields `false`.

---

## 2. The AvailabilityContext and where its fields come from

The context type is `ActionContext` (`action_registry.rs:43–81`). The two fields the dispatch closure consumes:

- **`lane: Lane`** (line 45) — "consumed from the ledger", built in `ActionContext::for_item` via `item.lane()` (line 92).
- **`surface: ActionSurface`** (line 80) — which per-item surface the selection lives on. `ActionSurface` (lines 29–35) has exactly two variants: `Attention` ("the needs-attention inbox with a work-item-backed row selected") and `LaneDrill` ("a drilled-in lane with an individual work-item selected").

**Where `surface` is populated** — `TuiModel::selected_action_context` in `/data/projects/livespec-console-beads-fabro/crates/console-application/src/lib.rs:2002–2021`:
```rust
let surface = match (self.active_view, self.lane_focus) {
    (TuiView::Attention, _) => action_registry::ActionSurface::Attention,
    (TuiView::Lanes, LaneFocus::Lane(_lane)) => action_registry::ActionSurface::LaneDrill,
    (TuiView::Lanes | TuiView::Spec | TuiView::Events | TuiView::Repos | TuiView::Settings, _) => return None,
};
...
action_registry::ActionContext::for_item(item, surface, ready_work_item_count)
```

So: **any selection made in the Attention view resolves to `ActionSurface::Attention`** — unconditionally, from the active view. This is *not* tied to admission policy, a pending-approval state, or an `awaits_scope_override` flag. Those other dimensions (`admission_policy`, `acceptance_policy`, `has_driver_handoff`, `awaits_scope_override`) exist on `ActionContext` and feed *other* actions (approve, driver-handoff, scope-override) but the dispatch closure ignores them entirely.

**What makes an Attention item "dispatchable":** nothing, through this action. Even a genuinely-Ready-lane work-item shown as an Attention row fails the `surface == LaneDrill` conjunct. Dispatchability here is a function of *which view the selection is on* plus *lane == ready*, not of any policy/lane-status admission gate. (An Attention row may still carry its own separate handoff — see §3/§4.)

---

## 3. Is dispatch wired to the orchestrator? — Yes, it is real, not a stub

The per-item dispatch is fully wired. The path from menu selection to command issue:

  not one. The mutation is EQUIVALENT - it changes no behaviour - and no test 
  can catch a change that changes nothing. The suite is not at fault, so

  exist.

  have to re-derive this analysis under time pressure, or - worse - will "fix"
  it by weakening a test. Two acceptable dispositions, and the choice belongs 
  with whoever does the work:

  (b) keep it as deliberate future-proofing (a DriverHandoff action might one 
  day be Attention-available) and add a justified-survivor allow-list entry   
  CITING THIS ITEM as the reason.

  The cockpit showed no indication whatsoever. I only discovered the failure  
  by

  fix.

  A dispatcher-policy edit made from the console Settings view is accepted,   
  persisted as a COMPLETED command AND a domain event, and then silently fails
  to                                                                          
  take effect. The Settings pane re-renders the OLD value, and the operator's 
  change is lost with no error.                                               
                                                                              
  ## Evidence (tenant livespec-console-beads-fabro, observed 2026-07-20)      
                                                                              
  Console store tmp/livespec-console.sqlite:                                  
                                                                              
  • commands row:                                                             
  cmd_config_dispatcher_setting_set_livespec-console-beads-fabro_wip_cap_6,   
  type config.dispatcher_setting_set, status **completed**,                   
  idempotency_key livespec-console-beads-fabro:config.                        
  dispatcher_setting_set:wip_cap=6,                                           
  payload {"repo":"livespec-console-beads-fabro","setting":"wip_cap",         
  "value":6},                                                                 
  result {"event_count":2}, requested_at 2026-07-19T07:55:42.772791591Z.      
  • events row: type config.dispatcher_setting.changed, payload               
  {"actor":"operator","new":6,"previous":5,"repo":"livespec-console-beads-    
  fabro","setting":"wip_cap","occurred_at":"2026-07-19T07:55:42.772791591Z"}.

  dispatcher block at all -- so the orchestrator's effective policy is the    
  built-in default, which is 5.                                               
                                                                              
  ## Reading of the defect                                                    
                                                                              
  The Settings pane reads the EFFECTIVE dispatcher policy (correctly showing  
  5),

  effective                                                                   
  policy. The write terminates inside the console's own event store. Net      
  effect:

  emitted

  the                                                                         
  console TUI" is the headline objective of the autonomous-mode programme     
  (livespec                                                                   
  core epic livespec-j4odoz).

Approve moves `pending-approval → ready`. The `PendingValve::Approve` variant doc says exactly that (`lib.rs:314`: "The approve human valve (`pending-approval -> ready`)"), and confirming persists a `WorkItemApproveRequested` command (`valve_outcome`, `lib.rs:4723-4728`).

Surface: **both Attention and LaneDrill.** Approve is *not* in the drill-only list (`action_registry.rs:1302-1306` lists only `move`, `driver-handoff`, `dispatch-selected-item`); its availability closure has no surface guard.

Important: approve applies to `pending-approval`, NOT to `backlog`. A backlog item is not in `pending-approval`, so `p` does nothing for it.

## 4. Lanes and navigation

The seven lanes, in canonical lifecycle order — `Lane::all()`, `source_adapters.rs:288-302`:

```rust
&[
    Self::Backlog,
    Self::PendingApproval,
    Self::Ready,
    Self::Active,
    Self::Acceptance,
    Self::Blocked,
    Self::Done,
]
```

Labels (`source_adapters.rs:306-315`): `backlog, pending-approval, ready, active, acceptance, blocked, done`. The doc at `source_adapters.rs:289-291` confirms "the lane board renders its columns in this order."

Views nav order — `TuiView::all()`, `console-application/src/lib.rs:160-169`: `Attention, Spec, **Lanes**, Events, Repos, Settings`.

Exact keystrokes:

- **Enter the Lanes view:** Focus starts on the Views nav (`FocusPane::Nav`). `Down`/`Up` move the Views selection — `down_interaction` → `SelectNextView`, `up_interaction` → `SelectPreviousView` (`console-tui/src/lib.rs:895` and `925`). Attention is index 0, Lanes is index 2, so from startup press **Down, Down** to land on Lanes.
- **Dive into the view's content:** with Lanes selected in Nav, `Enter` → `FocusContent` (`console-tui/src/lib.rs:964`).
- **Drill into a lane:** in the Content pane with `LaneFocus::Overview`, `Enter` → `DrillIntoLane` (`console-tui/src/lib.rs:966-970`).
- **Select an item within the drilled-in lane:** `Down`/`Up` → `SelectNext`/`SelectPrevious` (Content pane, `console-tui/src/lib.rs:896` and `926`).
- (Optional) `Enter` on a selected drilled-in item → `OpenWorkItemDetail` (a read-only detail modal, `console-tui/src/lib.rs:977-979`) — this is not required to run per-item actions; the cursor selection is what the `s`/`p`/`h` hotkeys act on.
- `Esc`/`Left` steps a drilled-in lane back to the overview (`content_back_interaction`, `console-tui/src/lib.rs:1018-1021`).

## 5. Bottom line — backlog item to ready, then dispatched

Assume the item starts in `backlog` and admission policy is the default (`Manual`).

Steps the TUI CAN do today:

1. **Navigate to the drilled-in backlog lane.** From startup: `Down Down` (select Lanes) → `Enter` (focus Content) → move to the Backlog lane → `Enter` (DrillIntoLane) → `Down`/`Up` to select the item. (Refs: `console-tui/src/lib.rs:895/925/964/966-970/896/926`.)
2. **Move `backlog → ready`.** Press **`s`** → the move valve opens staged to `backlog → ready` → `Enter` to confirm. This persists a `WorkItemMoveRequested { target_status: "ready" }` command. (Refs: `action_registry.rs:252-283`; `lib.rs:589`, `4804-4811`.)
   - Note: legality of the move is ultimately the orchestrator's authority (`lib.rs:4684-4686`), but the TUI offers and fires it.
3. **Dispatch the now-ready item.** After it is `ready`, in the drilled-in ready lane use the **`dispatch-selected-item`** action (`action_registry.rs:481-493`) — or `dispatch-ready` for the whole board (`471-480`). Confirming persists a `FactoryDispatchItemRequested` / `FactoryDrainRequested` command (`console-tui/src/lib.rs:633-640`; `lib.rs:4878-4886`).
   - **Caveat — no hotkey:** both dispatch actions have `hotkeys: &[]` / empty `hint_token`; they are menu/invoker-only. You must reach them via the **menu bar (`v`) → Factory → Dispatch**, or the **command palette (`:`, then type `actions`)**. There is no single-key dispatch. (Refs: `action_registry.rs:452-453/470-493`; palette-invoker at `lib.rs:4860-4862`.)

Steps the TUI CANNOT do today (require the orchestrator `drive` CLI / a driver skill run outside the TUI):

- **Grooming the backlog item** (turning a raw backlog item into groomed, ready-shaped slices) is NOT initiated in the TUI. Pressing **`h`** on a backlog item only copies the string `claude "/livespec-orchestrator-beads-fabro:groom <id>"` to your clipboard; you must run that skill elsewhere. (Refs: `lib.rs:4294-4321`, `711-718`; `console-tui/src/lib.rs:321-323/647-649/399-401`.) If your workflow requires grooming before an item is legitimately "ready," that grooming happens outside the TUI.
- **Implementing a factory-unsafe ready item** is likewise a copy-only handoff (`ready` + non-null `factory_safety` → `implement`), not a TUI-driven action (`lib.rs:4309`).
- The console never *executes* the drive itself in-process for these — valve/dispatch confirms **persist command envelopes** (`OperatorActionOutcome::PersistCommand`, `console-tui/src/lib.rs:675-682`); the underlying `drive --repo … --action …` execution is the orchestrator action port's job (`lib.rs:2811-2913`). What the TUI *guarantees* is that the move/approve/dispatch commands get issued; grooming and implementing are the two chain steps it can only hand off.

Also worth flagging: `p` (approve) is irrelevant to a plain `backlog` item — approve only fires from `pending-approval` (`lib.rs:604`). If your item never enters `pending-approval`, the `s` move to `ready` is the operative TUI step, not `p`.</result>

Verified against the code. Here's exactly what to do — keystroke by keystroke — with the two spots where the TUI hands off to something outside it flagged honestly.

## First, launch

```bash
just tui
```

Focus starts on the **Views** menu (left), with **Attention** selected.

---

## The one decision up front: groom, or move directly?

`1d5f` is already a single, dispatch-sized bug with a clear fix and acceptance — it does **not** strictly need grooming into slices. So the fastest real path is to move it straight to `ready` in the TUI. If you'd rather do the disciplined groom step first, that step is **not a TUI action** — see the note at the bottom.

---

## Exact keystrokes: backlog → ready → dispatch

### 1. Get to the item in the drilled-in Backlog lane
- `↓` `↓` — moves the Views selection Attention → Spec → **Lanes** (Lanes is 3rd)
- `Enter` — dives focus into the lane board (Content pane)
- `Enter` again — **Backlog is the leftmost lane and is selected by default**, so this drills into it
- `↓` / `↑` — move the cursor onto **`livespec-console-beads-fabro-1d5f`**

### 2. Move it `backlog → ready`
- `s` — opens the **Move status** valve, already staged to `backlog → ready` (backlog's first legal target is `ready`)
- `Enter` — confirms. This fires a `WorkItemMoveRequested { target_status: "ready" }` command to the orchestrator.
  - The modal parameter cycles `backlog / ready / blocked`; if it isn't showing **ready**, cycle to it before `Enter`.

### 3. Verify it actually landed in `ready` — do not skip this
- `Esc` — back out to the lane overview
- `→` (or navigate) to the **Ready** lane column → `Enter` to drill in
- Confirm `1d5f` now appears there.

**Why this step matters:** legality of the move is ultimately the *orchestrator's* call, not the console's — and if it rejects the move, the failure currently surfaces as **nothing** in the TUI (that's bug `k0w`, which you're aware of). So visually confirm rather than assume. If it did **not** move, fall back to grooming (bottom note).

### 4. Dispatch it — **note: there is no single-key dispatch**
With `1d5f` selected inside the drilled-in **Ready** lane:
- `v` — opens the menu bar
- `→` to **Factory**, then `↓` to **Dispatch**, `Enter` → pick **"Dispatch selected item"** → `Enter` to confirm

This fires `FactoryDispatchItemRequested`, and the orchestrator runs `dispatcher loop --repo <path> --budget 1 --parallel 1 --item livespec-console-beads-fabro-1d5f`.

**Simpler alternative** if `1d5f` is the only thing in Ready: `:` (command palette) → type `drain` → `Enter`. That drains the whole ready queue via `dispatch-ready`, which for a single ready item is the same effect and matches the documented quickstart.

---

## The step the TUI *cannot* do (be aware)

**Grooming is not a TUI action.** If you press `h` on the backlog item, it only **copies** the string `claude "/livespec-orchestrator-beads-fabro:groom livespec-console-beads-fabro-1d5f"` to your clipboard (OSC-52) — you'd paste and run that in a shell yourself. The TUI never runs the groomer. For `1d5f` you can skip grooming; but if step 3 shows the direct `s` move was refused, that's your signal the orchestrator wants the item groomed first — run that copied command outside the TUI, and any resulting slices will come back through the pipeline (landing in `pending-approval`, where `p` **approve** then promotes them to `ready`).

So the honest summary: **steps 1–4 are all real TUI actions and will issue real commands.** The only thing the TUI can't do for you is groom — and this particular item likely doesn't need it. Watch step 3 to know which world you're in.
